Construct a Sum of Quadratic Penalties

Source: R/additive_penalty.R
additive_penalty.Rd

Builds the Gaussian prior whose precision is a weighted sum of fixed positive semidefinite matrices, with one smoothing parameter for each matrix. An anisotropic tensor-product smooth uses this form: with one parameter per margin, the fit can be rough in one direction and smooth in another, whereas a single parameter smooths every direction alike.

Usage

additive_penalty(
  mats,
  map = NULL,
  blocks = 1L,
  readable = c("lambda", "sd"),
  link_lambda = linkfunctions7::log_link(),
  tol = 1e-10
)

Arguments

mats

A list of at least one symmetric positive semidefinite matrix, all with the same number of rows. Each component is symmetrized. A component is rejected with an error that gives its position when it has an entry that is not finite (NA, NaN or infinite), when it differs from its transpose by more than 1e-8 times the larger of 1 and its largest absolute entry, when its largest eigenvalue is not positive (a zero or negative semidefinite matrix), or when its smallest eigenvalue is below -tol times its largest. Under blocks > 1 they are the components of one block.

map

The matrix \(D\), with as many rows as each component has and one column per coefficient, or NULL (the default) for the identity. A map is absorbed at construction, and each component becomes \(D^\top P_kD\), so the stored map is always NULL and n_coef is the number of columns of the map. A map with an entry that is not finite is rejected, and so is a map that carries a component to the zero matrix, with an error that gives the position of that component.

blocks

How many times each component is repeated blockwise, a whole number of at least 1. 1L, the default, gives the ordinary penalty. A value above 1 cannot be combined with map.

readable

"lambda" (the default) or "sd", the quantities that penalty_readable() reports. See the section on the readable quantities.

link_lambda

The linkfunctions7 link that carries each smoothing parameter onto the whole real line, linkfunctions7::log_link() by default. The same link is used for every parameter.

tol

The relative eigenvalue tolerance, 1e-10 by default. It is used to reject a component whose smallest eigenvalue is below -tol times its largest, and to count the rank of the sum of the components after each has been divided by its largest absolute entry. The object stores tol, and additive_sum() passes it to additive_stable() as r_tol, so the rank of each group of components in the similarity transformation is counted at the same tolerance as the rank of the sum.

Value

An AdditivePenalty() object with one hyperparameter per component, named lambda1, lambda2, ... The hyperparameters are bounded on \((0, \infty)\).

The value

$$\rho(\beta;\lambda) = \tfrac{1}{2}\beta^\top S(\lambda)\beta - \tfrac{1}{2}\log\mathrm{pdet}\,S(\lambda) + \tfrac{r}{2}\log 2\pi, \qquad S(\lambda) = \sum_{k} \lambda_k P_k,$$

with \(r\) the rank of the sum. The hyperparameters are named lambda1, lambda2 and so on, in the order in which the components were given. Each is positive and is carried onto the real line by link_lambda, a log link by default.

The derivatives of the log pseudo-determinant

With \(S^{+}\) the pseudo-inverse of \(S(\lambda)\), the derivatives that a marginal criterion reads are traces against it:

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda_k}\log\mathrm{pdet}\,S = \operatorname{tr}(S^{+}P_k), \qquad \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\lambda_k\partial\lambda_l} \log\mathrm{pdet}\,S = -\operatorname{tr}(S^{+}P_kS^{+}P_l).$$

Both formulas are exact. additive_sum() evaluates the traces, together with the log pseudo-determinant, by the similarity transformation of additive_stable(), and never forms \(S^{+}\) itself.

The rank of the sum

The rank and the null basis are computed once, at construction, from the sum of the components after each has been divided by its largest absolute entry, and the rank is the number of eigenvalues of that sum above tol times the largest. Both are then fixed: the null space of \(S(\lambda)\) is the intersection of the null spaces of the components at every positive \(\lambda\). An eigenvalue count of the assembled \(S(\lambda)\) itself is correct only while the parameters are comparable. Once they differ by many orders of magnitude, the smaller contributions fall below any fixed relative tolerance and the count drops, although the stored null basis still annihilates the sum to rounding error.

Parameters that differ by many orders of magnitude

The stored rank fixes how many eigenvalues enter the log pseudo-determinant, but it does not make those eigenvalues computable from the assembled sum. When the parameters differ by enough orders of magnitude, the condition number of \(S(\lambda)\) exceeds \(1/\epsilon\) and the smallest eigenvalue on the range falls below the absolute accuracy of one symmetric eigendecomposition, which is of order \(d\,\epsilon\lVert S\rVert_{2}\). The log pseudo-determinant is therefore not taken, in general, from one decomposition of the assembled sum. additive_stable(), which additive_sum() calls, partitions the components by the size of their contributions and transforms by similarity, so that each decomposition resolves only the spread within one group of components. The sum is decomposed as a whole only when every contribution is at least additive_tol() times the largest, or when the dominant group by itself has the rank of the sum. The identities of the transformation are exact, and the accuracy of the value and of both derivative blocks is limited by the conditioning of the dominant group at each level of the partition rather than by the spread of the parameters. Where the weighted sum or one of its reductions overflows, or where the rank identity that additive_sum() checks at every call is violated or cannot be evaluated, the log pseudo-determinant and its derivatives are NaN, without an error. Such points become more frequent as the spread and the number of components grow.

The quantities of a marginal criterion

is_quadratic() returns TRUE, because a sum of quadratic forms is a quadratic form, so penalty_matrix(), penalty_rank(), penalty_null_basis() and penalty_logpdet() all have methods for this class, and check_penalty() runs its quadratic rows here (the row of the null basis only when the null basis has columns). The matrix moves with one hyperparameter per component, whereas the plain quadratic branch has a single scale, so the log pseudo-determinant is not linear in the logarithm of any one parameter. The row of check_penalty() that checks it therefore compares its gradient with numDeriv, where the plain quadratic branch checks a slope.

has_prox() returns FALSE. That function first tests whether the class registers a penalty_prox() method of its own, before it calls is_quadratic(), and this class registers none.

blocks = m builds the penalty whose components are \(I_m \otimes P_k\), which is the form of a smooth repeated once per group. The sum is \(I_m \otimes S_1(\lambda)\), with \(S_1\) the sum over one block, so its rank is \(m\) times the rank of the block, its log pseudo-determinant is \(m\log\mathrm{pdet}\,S_1(\lambda)\), and both derivative blocks are \(m\) times those of the block. The decomposition is taken on one block, and the repeated components are stored as sparse matrices, which is also the storage that penalty_hessian() and penalty_matrix() return. blocks cannot be combined with map.

The readable quantities

Setting readable = "sd" declares the smoothing parameters to be precisions of a prior, and penalty_readable() then reports the standard deviations \(\sigma_k = \lambda_k^{-1/2}\), named sigma1, sigma2 and so on, in place of the parameters. The penalty itself is unchanged.

See also

quadratic_penalty() for one matrix with one scale, structured_penalty() for a matrix whose entries move with the hyperparameters, penalty_logpdet.AdditivePenalty() for the log pseudo-determinant and its derivatives, additive_sum() for the computation that they share.

Examples

# This is an anisotropic tensor smooth over a 4 x 4 grid, and the curvature
# along each margin is penalized separately.
P <- crossprod(diff(diag(4), differences = 2))
pen <- additive_penalty(list(kronecker(diag(4), P), kronecker(P, diag(4))))
pen@params
#> [1] "lambda1" "lambda2"
c(n_coef = pen@n_coef, rank = penalty_rank(pen))
#> n_coef   rank 
#>     16     12 

# Raising one parameter penalizes roughness along that margin alone.
set.seed(2)
b <- rnorm(16)
penalty_value(pen, b, list(lambda1 = 1, lambda2 = 1))
#> [1] 66.29988
penalty_value(pen, b, list(lambda1 = 1, lambda2 = 100))
#> [1] 2292.209

# With one component the value is that of the plain quadratic penalty.
P2 <- crossprod(diff(diag(5), differences = 2))
bb <- c(0.4, -1.1, 0.7, 0.2, -0.3)
penalty_value(additive_penalty(list(P2)), bb, list(lambda1 = 3)) -
  penalty_value(quadratic_penalty(P2), bb, list(lambda = 3))
#> [1] 7.105427e-15

# The stored rank stays fixed as the parameters spread apart, while an
# eigenvalue count of the assembled sum drops.
a <- additive_penalty(list(crossprod(diff(diag(5))), P2))
penalty_rank(a)
#> [1] 4
sapply(c(1, 1e10), function(r) {
  S <- penalty_matrix(a, list(lambda1 = 1, lambda2 = r))
  ev <- eigen(S, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
  sum(ev > 1e-10 * max(ev))
})
#> [1] 4 3

# blocks = m repeats each component without decomposing the repetition.
rep4 <- additive_penalty(list(crossprod(diff(diag(5))), P2), blocks = 4)
c(n_coef = rep4@n_coef, rank = penalty_rank(rep4))
#> n_coef   rank 
#>     20     16 
th <- list(lambda1 = 2, lambda2 = 0.5)
penalty_logpdet(rep4, th)$value - 4 * penalty_logpdet(a, th)$value
#> [1] 0

# readable = "sd" reports the standard deviations of the prior.
sdp <- additive_penalty(list(diag(2), diag(c(1, 2))), readable = "sd")
penalty_readable(sdp, list(lambda1 = 4, lambda2 = 0.25))$value
#> sigma1 sigma2 
#>    0.5    2.0
